newsitem.title: USA: Fed faced with confusing economy, mulls rates.
newsitem.headline: Fed faced with confusing economy, mulls rates.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
Federal Reserve policymakers meet on Tuesday to consider increasing interest rates for the second time this year amid signs that U.S. economic growth is slowing but inflation risks are rising.
A slim majority of top bond dealers surveyed by Reuters -- 21 of 39 -- said they expect the central bank to opt to hold rates steady, at least for now.
"They won't do anything," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at St. Louis-based brokers A.G Edwards and Sons. "The Fed is going to wait a while to see how the economy develops."
The central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is scheduled to begin meeting at 9 a.m. (1300 GMT). It is expected to announce its decision at around 2:15 p.m. (1815 GMT).

At its last meeting on March 25, the inflation-wary Fed raised rates for the first time in more than two years, bumping up the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point. The funds rate -- the rate commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans -- now stands at 5.5 percent.
Arguing for another rate rise: an economy that has been growing too quickly for its own good, a tight jobs market, rising wages and a stock market that may be too exuberant.
Arguing against: an expected slowdown in the economy, scant sign of any pick-up in inflation, increased worker productivity and spare capacity in the industrial sector.
A rate rise would mean higher borrowing costs for everyone from consumers using credit cards to the stores where they shop. It would tend to slow the economy and dampen inflation.
White House chief economist Janet Yellen steered clear on Monday of commenting on the Fed's policies. But she did say that she saw no sign of any pick-up in inflation.
"There is no evidence at this point of inflationary pressure," Yellen, a former Fed Governor, told a meeting sponsored by the Center for National Policy think tank.
She added that there was a "great deal of uncertainty" now about how the economy is operating.

The unemployment rate has fallen to levels that in the past led workers to demand hefty increases in wages and benefits, ultimately leading to higher inflation. But that has not occurred this time, at least so far. The jobless rate in April was 4.9 percent, its lowest level in nearly 24 years.
Wall Street stock prices rose on Monday ahead of the Fed meeting, with the Dow Jones industrial average of blue chip shares ending the day 34.21 points higher at 7,228.88. Bond prices eased slightly.
Traders were optimistic that a modest rise in rates would not crimp stock prices.

Frank Calta, a trader at broker Dain Bosworth, said, "If the FOMC raises rates by 25 basis points (a quarter percentage point), it's ... not a big deal. If they don't raise rates, it's a positive, but not a blowout positive."

But the reaction elsewhere to a rate rise is likely to be more explosive. An unusual alliance of corporations and labor unions, conservatives and liberals is already lining up to attack the Fed if it decides to tighten credit further.
Jerry Jasinowski, President of the National Association of Manufacturers, said on Monday he saw no need for the Fed to raise rates, arguing that the economy is slowing on its own.

In a speech in New York earlier this month, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan vociferously defended the March rate increase, calling it a prudent step to guard against inflation and likening it to a vaccination to prevent a serious disease.
But he steered clear of spelling out what he intends to do on Tuesday, although he did say the Fed would need to raise rates again if economic growth fails to slow down as expected.

Growth does seem to be moderating from its rapid rate in the first quarter, when the economy expanded at its fastest clip in more than nine years. Sales at retail stores dropped in April and industrial production was flat.
"I don't think the Fed wants to be perceived as trying to kill the economy," Thayer, of A.G. Edwards and Sons, said.
But it is not clear how long the expected second quarter slowdown will last, analysts said. Jobs are plentiful and consumers are confident, pointing to the possibility of a pick-up later this year.
